Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

which pronoun

the one that (relative)

also that (relative), who (relative), whom (relative), whose (relative), the one which

classical

Catull. 3.5: quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat
Phaedr. 1 prol. 1: Aesōpus auctor quam māteriam repperit

quī, quae, quod

relative pronoun: gender and number from the word it refers to, case from its own clause, declension

who, which, that

English may leave the relative out (“the boat you see”); Latin never does. Its genitive cujus, quōrum, quārum is “whose”, its dative cui, quibus “to whom”. At the head of a sentence it links back where English says “and he”, “and this”: quā lēctā, and when I had read it (Cic. Att. 12.1.2).

Examples

  • passer mortuus est meae puellae, passer, dēliciae meae puellae, quem plūs illa oculīs suīs amābat

    my girl’s sparrow is dead, the sparrow, my girl’s delight, whom she loved more than her own eyesCatull. 3.3–5

  • Aesōpus auctor quam māteriam repperit, hanc ego polīvī versibus sēnāriīs

    the material that Aesop the author found, I have polished in iambic versePhaedr. 1 prol. 1–2

  • cum complicārem hanc epistulam, noctuābundus ad mē vēnit cum epistulā tuā tabellārius; quā lēctā dē Atticae febriculā scīlicet valdē doluī.

    As I was folding this letter, the courier came to me by night with yours; when I had read it, I was of course very sorry about Attica’s touch of fever.Cic. Att. 12.1.2

  • vīvitur parvō bene, cui paternum splendet in mēnsā tenuī salīnum

    he lives well on little whose father’s salt-cellar shines on his plain tableHor. C. 2.16.13–14

  • aper … pilleātus, ē cujus dentibus sportellae dēpendēbant duae palmulīs textae

    a boar wearing a freedman’s cap, from whose tusks hung two little baskets woven of palmPetr. 40.1

See also which, who, whose, that.
